etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English lawier, lawyer, lawer, equivalent to law +‎ -yer.

definitions.definition: A professional person with a graduate law degree that qualifies for legal work (such as Juris Doctor)

A professional person qualified (as by a law degree or bar exam) and authorized to practice law as an attorney-at-law, solicitor, advocate, barrister or equivalent, i.e. represent parties in lawsuits or trials and give legal advice.

quote.citation: 1907 August, Robert W[illiam] Chambers, chapter II, in The Younger Set, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: His forefathers had been, as a rule, professional men—physicians and lawyers; his grandfather died under the walls of Chapultepec Castle while twisting a tourniquet for a cursing dragoon; an uncle remained indefinitely at Malvern Hill; […].

definitions.definition: (by extension) A legal layman who argues points of law.
(UK, dialect) The stem of a bramble.
A relative of the raspberry found in Australia and New Zealand, Rubus australis

quote.citation: 1881 April, George M. Thomson, “On the Fertilization of New Zealand Flowering Plants”, in Transactions and Proceedings of the New Zealand Institute, volume 13, page 250:
quote.text: The species of Eugnomus are very partial to the lawyer (Rubus australis ) when in bloom.

quote.citation: 1885, New Zealand Journal of Science - Volume 2, page 417:
quote.text: In the lawyer (Rubus australis) a considerable differentiation has taken place. All the alllies of this plant (such as the true roses, brambles, rasps, &c.), exhibit a strong development of epidermal structures in the form of hooks, spines, or hairs, but in none are these structures so perfect as in our lawyer.

quote.citation: 1915, John Henderson, P. Marshall, Percy Gates Morgan, The Geology and Mineral Resources of the Reefton Subdivision, Westport and North Westland Division, page 6:
quote.text: A plant that is excessively troublesome in the localities where the native vegetation has been least disturbed is the “lawyer” (Rubus australis).

definitions.definition: Various species of Calamus, including Calamus australis, Calamus muelleri, Calamus obstruens, Calamus vitiensis, Calamus warburgii, and Calamus moti.

quote.citation: 1886, Edward Micklethwaite Curr, The Australian Race, page 427:
quote.text: Besides the bags and nets common throughout the continent, these tribes have water-bags, which they make of closely-plaited “lawyer” (Calamus Australis), and also of palm-leaf sewn with the sinews of animals.

quote.citation: 1901, Archibald James Campbell, Nests and Eggs of Australian Birds, page 267:
quote.text: The nest was a foot or two from the ground, and placed in a bunch of lawyer (Calamus ) canes.

quote.citation: 1905, W. J. Gordon, “Jackey Jackey”, in The Boy's Own Annual, volume 28, page 318:
quote.text: This lawyer (Calamus australis) is a climbing palm, throwing up shoots from its roots as thick as a man's finger and tough as wire, covered with sharp spines, and bearing much divided leaves, alternating with tendrils twenty feel long.

quote.citation: 1910 October, Sidney Wm. Jackson, “Additional Notes on Tooth-billed Bower-Bird (Scenopaeetes dentirostris) of North Queensland”, in The Emu: Official Organ of the Australasian Ornithologists' Union, volume 10, page 84:
quote.text: They were usually very neatly laid out under arching masses of the exasperating lawyer-palm vines ( Calamus moti and C. australis ), and consequently not too easy to examine.

quote.citation: 2014, Germaine Greer, White Beech: The Rainforest Years, page 171:
quote.text: Lawyer Vine (Calamus muelleri), also known as Hairy Mary and Wait-a-while, is actually a palm, that grows in long canes that loop and snake through the undergrowth.

quote.citation: 2022, E. J. Banfield, The Confessions of a Beachcomber:
quote.text: The trail of the lawyer vine (CALAMUS OBSTRUENS), with its leaf sheath and long tentacles bristling  with incurved hooks, is over it all.

definitions.definition: A woody climbing rainforest vine, Flagellaria indica.

quote.citation: 2011, A. C. Haddon, W. H. R. Rivers, Reports of the Cambridge Anthropological Expedition to Torres Straits, page 89:
quote.text: The stems of the "lawyer vine" (Flagellaria indica), buz or buzi (W.), boz (E.), are used in house-building, tying fences, etc.

definitions.definition: Any of various plants that have hooked thorns.
(intransitive) To perform, or attempt to perform, the work of a lawyer.
(informal, transitive) To barrage (a person) with questions in order to get them to admit something.
